r0.why: Mineral and main iron ore [1], oxide of iron [2], black or brownish-black, metallic luster, hardness 5-6, black streak [5], IUPAC and common chemical names [7].

r1.why: Attracted to a magnet and can become a permanent magnet [2], most magnetic bar rare native iron [3], lodestone attracting iron and discovery of magnetism [4], early compass [34].

r2.why: Small grains common in igneous and metamorphic rocks [6], sedimentary rocks, banded iron formations, lake and marine sediments [8], beach sand [44], the three named places [45], aeromagnetic surveys with magnetometer [42].

r3.why: Composition formula [10], ferrous and ferric iron suggesting intermediate oxygen [11], structure established 1915 [12], one of the first by X-ray diffraction [13].

r4.why: Importance for rock-forming conditions [24], reacts with oxygen to hematite and forms buffer controlling oxygen fugacity [25], HM buffer [26], QFM with quartz and fayalite at lower oxygen [27], QFM close to most igneous rocks [30].

r5.why: Critical tool in paleomagnetism, important for plate tectonics [35]; relationships with ilmenite, hematite, ulvospinel much studied and reactions with oxygen affect the magnetic record [36].
